issues.legal_issue: An uncorroborated tape recording, without testimony establishing the recorded conversation, is not proper evidence of that conversation in a rent-eviction proceeding.
material_facts: The Rent Controller relied essentially on a tape-recorded conversation to find that a subtenant had been inducted after the contractual tenancy ended.
No participant in the conversation, and no person who overheard it, gave evidence establishing that the conversation had taken place.
There was no other proper evidence supporting the finding of a later subletting.
issues.conclusion: The tape recording could not be relied on by itself as proper evidence, and the finding that a subtenant was inducted after the contractual tenancy ended was unsupported.
issues.legal_principle: A tape-recorded conversation is usable as corroborative evidence of a conversation testified to by a participant or an overhearer; without such testimony it is not proper evidence. The Court relied on S. Pratap Singh v. The State of Punjab.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant on a ground relating to subletting.
predicates.tape_recording_offered_as_proof: A party relies on a tape recording to prove that a conversation occurred or what was said in it.
predicates.no_witness_established_conversation: No participant in the recorded conversation and no person who overheard it testified to establish the conversation.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding relies on a tape recording but no witness establishes the conversation, the recording is not proper evidence by itself.

issues.legal_issue: A subletting created with the landlord’s written consent while the contractual tenancy subsists does not become unauthorized merely because the contractual tenancy later ends, and continued possession by the lawfully inducted subtenant does not itself establish a new subletting.
material_facts: The written rent agreement authorized the tenant to sublet specified portions of the premises.
The subtenants were inducted in April, while the contractual tenancy was subsisting and the landlord’s written consent was in force.
The finding that further subletting occurred after the contractual tenancy ended was unsupported by proper evidence.
The subtenants continued in possession after the contractual tenancy ended.
issues.conclusion: The tenant had not sublet any portion without the landlord’s written consent, so the landlord had no ground to evict the tenant for subletting; the eviction order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 makes unauthorized subletting after commencement of the Act a ground for eviction. Read with the Act’s definitions of landlord and tenant in sections 2(c) and 2(i), a subtenant inducted lawfully with written consent is a tenant under the Act and receives its protection against eviction. Continued possession after the contractual tenancy ends is not a fresh subletting. The judgment discusses V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal and Damadilal v. Parashram in relation to protection after contractual tenancy; it does not decide whether a tenant may create a new subtenancy after that tenancy ends.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and written_subletting_consent and subtenant_inducted_during_contractual_tenancy and no_fresh_unauthorized_subletting

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant on a ground relating to subletting.
predicates.written_subletting_consent: The landlord gave written consent for the tenant to sublet the relevant portion.
predicates.subtenant_inducted_during_contractual_te: The tenant inducted the subtenant while the contractual tenancy was still subsisting.
predicates.no_fresh_unauthorized_subletting: After the original lawful subletting, the tenant did not create a new subletting without the landlord’s written consent; the subtenant’s continued possession alone did not involve a new induction.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding concerns a subtenant inducted during the contractual tenancy with written consent and no fresh unauthorized subletting occurs, the tenant is not evictable on the subletting ground.
